title: Secure Service Mesh Reference for Private Deployments
author: Avery Chen
content:
Summary:
This reference describes a production-ready, security-first service mesh architecture tailored for Redwood Inference private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It includes recommended topology, network requirements, TLS/KMS patterns, RBAC guardrails, operational runloops, upgrade and rollback guidance, and a validation checklist operators can use during install and day-2 operations.

Scope and intended audience:
- Scope: Private deployments only (VPC & on-prem packaged installs). Does NOT cover hosted API routing or Dedicated multi-tenant pools.
- Audience: Platform engineers, deployment engineers, SREs, and customer engineers running private instances.

Goals and design principles:
- Zero-trust by default: mTLS between all platform control and data plane components.
- Minimal lateral blast radius: strict service identity and RBAC enforced at mesh gateways and sidecars.
- Observable and debuggable: standardized tracing, metrics, and structured logs from mesh proxies.
- Upgrade-safe: clear version skew tolerances and automated rollback hooks.

High-level topology (textual diagram):
- Control plane (single active / single-writer per deployment): redwood-control-plane (accepts admin, model onboarding, rollout API)
- Data plane (many): runtime-sidecars attached to model workers, proxying ingress/egress through mesh gateway
- Mesh ingress: edge-gateway (North-South, TLS termination optional depending on customer)
- Service-to-service: sidecars + Envoy-based listener chain, egress through egress-gateway to external services (KMS, container registry)
- Observability: telemetry-collector -> internal observability cluster (Prometheus remote_write, OTLP tracing to local or customer backend)

Core components and recommended implementations:
- Control plane: redwood-control-plane service (k8s deployment or systemd-backed on prem). Provide a single logical instance with active/standby leader election.
- Service mesh: Envoy proxies as sidecars + control plane using Istio 1.x or lightweight alternative (Consul Connect or Linkerd) depending on SLO for CPU overhead. We recommend Envoy-based mesh for feature parity with existing runtime routing.
- Ingress gateway: Envoy edge-gateway configured with SNI routing and TLS passthrough where customers manage certs.
- Egress gateway: central egress for external dependencies; all egress must be ACL'ed.
- Identity: SPIFFE-based service identity with short-lived mTLS certs; integrate with customer PKI or Redwood KMS if allowed.
- Key management: KMS/HSM-backed secrets for model keys; KMS endpoints only reachable via egress gateway.

Network and firewall requirements (table):
- Control plane -> Worker sidecars: TCP 15001-15010 (mesh data/management), UDP ephemeral for health checks
- Ingress -> edge-gateway: TCP 443
- edge-gateway -> control-plane API: TCP 8443
- Egress gateway -> KMS/Registry: customer-specific ports (typically 443)
- Node-to-node: SSH 22 (admin), kubelet 10250 (k8s) where applicable

(Operators should map these to cloud security groups / on-prem ACLs.)

Configuration snippets (Envoy listener example):
- example Listener (pseudo YAML):
  listeners:
    - name: mesh-inbound
      address: 0.0.0.0:15001
      filters:
        - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
          typed_config: { ... }

Identity and secrets pattern:
1) Bootstrapping: node agent authenticates to Redwood control-plane using a one-time enrollment token (signed by customer PKI).
2) The control-plane mints short-lived SPIFFE identities (TTL 1h) for sidecars.
3) Secrets (model keys, DB creds) are vaulted in customer KMS and injected via sidecar secret-syncer on demand.

RBAC and policy recommendations:
- Default deny for all inter-service calls.
- Explicit allow lists per service: example redwood-control-plane -> model-store (GET/POST) allowed; runtime-sidecar -> kv-cache allowed only for model inference sessions.
- Administrative endpoints only reachable from operator CIDR (separate VPN).

SLOs and performance impact guidance:
- Target added p99 tail latency for inference path from request ingress to first token = +2–5ms for sidecar proxying (depends on probe frequency and batching).
- CPU overhead: expect 5–12% CPU increase on worker nodes with Envoy sidecar in optimized build. Use profiling to tune batching thresholds.

Installation and operator checklist (numbered procedure):
1) Preflight: validate node time sync (chrony/ntp), kernel settings for high file descriptors (> 200k), and NIC offload settings.
2) Network: ensure ports/open ACLs per the Network table.
3) Provision bootstrap token and customer PKI or configure Redwood KMS endpoint.
4) Deploy control plane (single active): verify readiness endpoint /health returns 200 and version header.
5) Install mesh control plane and sidecar injector. Validate injection with sample workload.
6) Configure ingress and egress gateways with TLS certs and ACLs.
7) Deploy observability collectors and confirm metrics/traces are flowing.
8) Run validation-suite (see Validation checklist).

Validation checklist (commands and expected outputs):
- Mesh connectivity test:
  - curl -v --resolve inference.redwood.internal:443:10.0.0.12 https://inference.redwood.internal/health
  - Expected: HTTP/2 200, body {"status":"ok"}
- mTLS verification:
  - Use spirectl or equivalent to inspect x509 SAN: spiffe://redwood/<service>/<instance>
  - Expected: Certificate SAN contains SPIFFE ID and TTL < 3600s
- RBAC test (negative):
  - From runtime-sidecar simulate call to control-plane admin endpoint -> curl https://control-plane.internal/admin
  - Expected: HTTP 403 (default deny)
- Observability smoke test:
  - Query Prometheus for mesh_request_total for service=redwood-runtime > 0 after synthetic load for 60s

Upgrade and rollback guidance (short):
- Version policy: control-plane and mesh control plane must be upgraded in a 2-step process: control-plane -> mesh-control-plane -> sidecars. Avoid skipping more than one minor version.
- Canary rollout: enable canary label on 5% of runtime nodes and verify health/metrics for 30m.
- Rollback trigger conditions: error rate increase > 2x baseline for 15m or tail-latency regression > 25% p99.
- Automated rollback: deployment controller will revert sidecar injector but operators must run the following steps to drain nodes safely:
  1. Mark node unschedulable
  2. Drain pods with PodDisruptionBudget overrides for critical workloads
  3. Reapply previous sidecar image tag

Day-2 operations and runloops:
- Cert rotation: rotate SPIFFE root every 30 days; automated via control-plane cert-rotator job. Verify rotation window using cert-rotation-status endpoint.
- Scaling: use autoscaler on runtime pods but ensure sidecar CPU limits are provisioned to avoid eviction ripple.
- Capacity reclaim: enable prefix/KV cache eviction policies when memory pressure > 70%
- Incident runbook summary: for mesh-induced incidents see Runbook ID: RB-MESH-2025 (link in related_pages).

Troubleshooting common failure modes:
- Symptom: mTLS handshake failures across nodes -> check clock skew, CA root distribution, and network MTU mismatches
- Symptom: Increased tail latency after sidecar injection -> profile Envoy filter chains, disable heavy access logs, validate TCP keepalive settings
- Symptom: Observability gaps -> confirm telemetry-collector has correct OTLP endpoint and no egress ACL blocking

Security considerations and customer controls:
- Audit logging: all control plane mutating APIs must be recorded and forwarded to customer SIEM; use append-only storage with 365-day retention for enterprise customers.
- Data residency: model artifacts must remain on customer storage; ensure egress ACLs prevent accidental push to external S3 buckets.
- Customer-managed KMS preference: if customer requires HSM, configure egress gateway policy to only allow KMS endpoints from HSM IP addresses.

Owners, escalation, and links:
- Architecture owner: Avery Chen (platform-arch@redwood.ai)
- Primary oncall for mesh incidents: eng-sre team (pager duty: #redwood-mesh-oncall)
- Related runbooks and playbooks: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/runtime-observability-capacity-and-spot-recovery-guide-2025

Appendix: sample sidecar resource limits (YAML snippet):
- resources:
    limits:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    requests:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: "256Mi"

Appendix: quick verification script (pseudo-bash):
- set -e
- curl -fsS https://control-plane.internal/health || { echo 'control-plane down'; exit 1; }
- spirectl svid show || { echo 'identity problem'; exit 2; }
- kubectl get pods -n redwood | grep -v Running && exit 3

Notes and rationale:
- We adopted SPIFFE and Envoy to align with the runtime's requirement for short-lived identities and advanced routing capabilities. Lightweight meshes may be acceptable for latency-sensitive customers but increase operational divergence.
